title: Sēf's neighbourhood
goal: Sēf shows you round his family's neighbourhood: talk about the houses and the people
tip: Many plurals change inside the word, so learn them in pairs: bēt → byūt, rayyāl → ryāyīl, bint → banāt. Most adjectives for people take -īn: nās ṭayybīn. For things, use the feminine: il-byūt kbīra 'the houses are big', killha 'all of them'. Two is still -ēn: waladēn.
grammar: broken plurals (bēt → byūt, rayyāl → ryāyīl, bint → banāt); people take -īn
dialogue: A
هذا فريجنا. هذي البيوت كلها حق أهلي
hādha firījna. hādhi l-byūt killha ḥagg ahli
This is our neighbourhood. These houses all belong to my family.
B
ما شاء الله! البيوت كبيرة وايد
mā shāʼ allāh! il-byūt kbīra wāyid
Wow! The houses are really big.
A
هيه. هذا بيت يدي، عنده خمس بنات وولدين
hē. hādha bēt yaddi, ʿindah khams banāt w waladēn
Yes. This is my grandad's house. He's got five daughters and two sons.
B
ومنو هذيلا الرياييل اللي في الشارع؟
w minu hādhēla r-ryāyīl illi fi sh-shāriʿ?
And who are these men in the street?
A
عيال عمي. ناس طيبين، كل واحد ريّال زين
ʿyāl ʿammi. nās ṭayybīn, kill wāḥid rayyāl zēn
My cousins. Nice people, every one of them a good guy.
B
الفريج حلو! والناس يعرفون بعض؟
il-firīj ḥilu! w in-nās yaʿarfūn baʿaẓ?
It's a lovely neighbourhood! And do people know each other?
A
هيه، كلهم أهل وجيران
hē, killhum ahal w jīrān
Yes, they're all family and neighbours.
items: one: rayyāl (ريّال); you'll see written ريايل
one: wild ʿammi (ولد عمي); my uncle's daughters: banāt ʿammi (بنات عمي)
all of them (things); all of it
big (with a feminine noun or a plural of things)
masculine: kbīr (كبير); il-byūt kbīra 'the houses are big'

title: Shops in Deira
goal: At work, Maryam tells you where she shops: talk about shops, souqs and streets
tip: Words in -a add -āt: sayyāra → sayyārāt; so do some others, maḥall → maḥallāt. Other plurals are broken: sūg → aswāg, ʿiṭir → ʿuṭūr, maṭʿam → maṭāʿim. Plurals of things take a feminine singular adjective: il-maḥallāt ghālya 'the shops are expensive'.
grammar: sound plurals -āt (sayyāra → sayyārāt); plural things take a feminine adjective
dialogue: A
وين تشتري أغراضك؟ من المول؟
wēn tishtiri aghrāẓak? min il-mōl?
Where do you buy your stuff? At the mall?
B
هيه، بس المحلات في المول غالية. وانتي؟
hē, bas il-maḥallāt fi l-mōl ghālya. w inti?
Yes, but the shops in the mall are expensive. And you?
A
أنا أروح ديرة. الأسواق هناك أرخص بوايد
ana arūḥ Dēra. il-aswāg hnāk arkhaṣ b-wāyid
I go to Deira. The souqs there are much cheaper.
B
والله؟ شو تشترين من هناك؟
wallāh? shu tishtirīn min hnāk?
Really? What do you buy there?
A
كل شي! فيها عطور وملابس ومطاعم وايد
kill shay! fīha ʿuṭūr w malābis w maṭāʿim wāyid
Everything! There are perfumes, clothes and loads of restaurants.
B
حلو! بس الشوارع هناك زحمة، صح؟
ḥilu! bas ish-shawāriʿ hnāk zaḥma, ṣaḥḥ?
Nice! But the streets there are busy, right?
A
هيه، الناس وايد، والسيارات بعد. روح بالمترو
hē, in-nās wāyid, w is-sayyārāt baʿad. rūḥ bil-mitrō
Yes, there are loads of people, and cars too. Go by metro.
items: there is, there are (in it: a feminine place, such as a city or an area)
for a masculine place: fīh (فيه); fīha maḥallāt 'it has shops'

title: Iftar at Sēf's
goal: Sēf invites you to break the fast at his family's house: give and answer the Ramadan greetings
tip: Ramadan greetings come in pairs. mubārak ʿalēkum ish-shahar → allāh ybārik fīk. ramaẓān karīm → allāhu akram. After breaking the fast or after prayer: tagabbal allāh → minna w minkum. Plurals again: killna ṣāymīn 'we're all fasting'.
grammar: recycle: plurals (ṣāymīn, yōʿānīn) with Ramadan greetings and their replies
dialogue: A
هلا والله! حياك الله، تفضل
hala wallāh! ḥayyāk allāh, tfaẓẓal
Hey! Welcome, come in.
B
هلا فيك، الله يحييك. مبارك عليكم الشهر!
hala fīk, allāh yḥayyīk. mubārak ʿalēkum ish-shahar!
Hi, thanks. Happy Ramadan to you all!
A
الله يبارك فيك. رمضان كريم! الفطور جاهز
allāh ybārik fīk. ramaẓān karīm! il-fuṭūr jāhiz
And to you. Ramadan Kareem! Iftar's ready.
B
الله أكرم. أنا صايم، والحين تعبان ويوعان!
allāhu akram. ana ṣāyim, w il-ḥīn taʿbān w yōʿān!
God is more generous. I'm fasting, and by now I'm tired and starving!
A
كلنا صايمين ويوعانين! يلا، أذن المغرب. خذ تمر وماي
killna ṣāymīn w yōʿānīn! yalla, adhdhan il-maghrib. khudh tamr w māy
We're all fasting and starving! Right, the maghrib call's gone. Have some dates and water.
B
الحمد لله. تقبل الله
il-ḥamdu lillāh. tagabbal allāh
Thank God. May God accept (our fast).
A
منا ومنكم. يلا نصلي قبل الأكل
minna w minkum. yalla nṣalli gabil il-akil
From us and from you. Come on, let's pray before we eat.
items: happy Ramadan (lit. blessed be the month for you), at the start of Ramadan
said as it is, to one person or many; the reply is allāh ybārik fīk (to a woman: fīch)
God is more generous (the reply to ramaẓān karīm)
may God accept (it), said after breaking the fast or after prayer
the reply is minna w minkum
from us and from you (the reply to tagabbal allāh)
a woman: ṣāyma (صايمة); a group: ṣāymīn (صايمين)
iftar, the meal that breaks the fast
fuṭūr also means breakfast; breakfast is also riyūg (ريوق)
the maghrib call to prayer has gone (time to break the fast)
culture: Ramadan greetings are everyday speech, not formal. At the start of the month you'll hear mubārak ʿalēkum ish-shahar, and ramaẓān karīm all month. The fast ends at the maghrib call to prayer. People usually break it with dates and water, pray maghrib, and then eat.

title: Back after Eid
goal: At the office after the Eid holiday, Maryam welcomes you back: Eid greetings and the summer weather
tip: For Eid, say ʿasākum min ʿuwwādah and answer by saying it back. To someone back from a trip: il-ḥamdu lillāh ʿala s-salāma → allāh ysallmak (to a woman: ysallmich). Plural things still take the feminine: ish-shawāriʿ w is-sayyārāt killha ghubār 'the streets and cars are all covered in dust'.
grammar: recycle: plurals with feminine agreement (ish-shawāriʿ killha)
dialogue: A
هلا! عساكم من عواده
hala! ʿasākum min ʿuwwādah
Hi! Happy Eid (lit. may you see it come back).
B
هلا فيج! عساكم من عواده
hala fīch! ʿasākum min ʿuwwādah
Hi! Happy Eid to you too.
A
وين كنت في العيد؟ ما شفناك
wēn kint fi l-ʿīd? ma shifnāk
Where were you over Eid? We didn't see you.
B
سافرت لندن عند أهلي. رجعت أمس
sāfart Landan ʿind ahli. rijaʿt ams
I flew to London, to my family. I got back yesterday.
A
الحمد لله على السلامة! شحال الأهل؟
il-ḥamdu lillāh ʿala s-salāma! shḥāl il-ahal?
Welcome back! How's the family?
B
الله يسلمج، كلهم بخير. بس الرطوبة هني!
allāh ysallmich, killhum b-khēr. bas ir-ruṭūba hni!
Thanks, they're all well. But the humidity here!
A
والغبار بعد! الشوارع والسيارات كلها غبار
w il-ghubār baʿad! ish-shawāriʿ w is-sayyārāt killha ghubār
And the dust too! The streets and the cars are all covered in dust.
items: happy Eid (lit. may you be among those who see it again)
عيد مبارك / كل عام وأنتم بخير
the reply is the same words
welcome back (from a trip or an illness; lit. thank God you're safe)
the reply is allāh ysallmak (to a woman: allāh ysallmich)
I travelled, I went away; you travelled (to a man)
at my family's, (staying) with my family
we didn't see you, we haven't seen you (to a man)
to a woman: ma shifnāch (ما شفناج)

title: What do I call him?
goal: Outside Bū Rāshid's majlis in Sharjah, Sēf tells you how to address his uncle
tip: gūl 'say' takes -lah 'to him': gūl-lah 'tell him', la tgūl-lah 'don't say to him', shu agūl-lah? 'what do I call him?'. Call an older man yā Bū Rāshid, yā ʿammi or ṭāl ʿumrak, even if he isn't your uncle. yā rayyāl is for friends only.
dialogue: A
وصلنا. هذا مجلس عمي بو راشد. الرياييل كلهم داخل
wiṣalna. hādha majlis ʿammi Bū Rāshid. ir-ryāyīl killhum dākhil
We're here. This is my uncle Bū Rāshid's majlis. All the men are inside.
B
شو أقول له؟ يا بو راشد؟
shu agūl-lah? yā Bū Rāshid?
What do I call him? Bū Rāshid?
A
عادي. أو قول له يا عمي، أو طال عمرك
ʿādi. aw gūl-lah yā ʿammi, aw ṭāl ʿumrak
That's fine. Or call him 'uncle', or 'sir'.
B
ويا ريّال؟ مثل ما أقول لك؟
w yā rayyāl? mithil ma agūl-lak?
And 'yā rayyāl'? Like I say to you?
A
لا تقول له يا ريّال! هذي حق الشباب، مب الكبار
la tgūl-lah yā rayyāl! hādhi ḥagg ish-shabāb, mub il-kbār
Don't call him 'yā rayyāl'! That's for the guys, not for older people.
B
زين. وإذا قال لي الحمد لله على السلامة؟
zēn. w idha gāl-li l-ḥamdu lillāh ʿala s-salāma?
OK. And if he says 'welcome back' to me?
A
قول له الله يسلمك يا طويل العمر. ناس طيبين، بتشوف
gūl-lah allāh ysallmak yā ṭawīl il-ʿumr. nās ṭayybīn, bitshūf
Say 'allāh ysallmak, ṭawīl il-ʿumr' to him. They're nice people, you'll see.
items: uncle, sir (respectful, to any older man)
not only for your real uncle
sir (respectful; lit. may your life be long) (to a man)
to a woman: ṭāl ʿumrich (طال عمرج)
sir (respectful, to an elder; lit. long-lived one) (to a man)
to a woman: ṭawīlat il-ʿumr (طويلة العمر); usually yā ṭawīl il-ʿumr; a mark of respect, not a title
tell him, say to him (to a man)
what do I say to him? what do I call him?
don't tell him, don't say to him (to a man)
to a woman: la tgūlīn-lah (لا تقولين له)
mithil ma agūl-lak 'the way I say it to you'
culture: yā rayyāl is for friends. Saying it to an elder or in a meeting is a real social mistake. Older men are yā ʿammi, whether or not they're your uncle. ṭawīl il-ʿumr and ṭāl ʿumrak wish someone a long life. They show respect to elders, strangers and sheikhs, and they aren't a title.

title: Coffee in the majlis
goal: Bū Rāshid welcomes you and serves Arabic coffee: accept a cup, and say when you've had enough
tip: A host gives orders with imperatives: tfaẓẓal igʿid 'please sit', yīb id-dalla 'bring the pot', ṣubb-lah 'pour (for) him'. ṣubb is a doubled verb like ḥuṭṭ 'put'. To refuse more, say bas, mashkūr and shake the cup.
grammar: recycle: imperatives (tfaẓẓal igʿid, yīb, ṣubb-lah) and object -ha (aḥibbha)
dialogue: A
هلا والله! حياك الله يا ولدي
hala wallāh! ḥayyāk allāh yā wildi
Hello there! Welcome, son.
B
هلا فيك. الله يحييك يا عمي
hala fīk. allāh yḥayyīk yā ʿammi
Hello. Thank you, uncle.
A
تفضل اقعد. سيف، ييب الدلة وصب له
tfaẓẓal igʿid. Sēf, yīb id-dalla w ṣubb-lah
Please, sit down. Sēf, bring the coffee pot and pour him some.
B
القهوة العربية أحبها وايد
il-gahwa l-ʿarabiyya aḥibbha wāyid
I love Arabic coffee.
A
خذ تمر ويا الفنجان. تبي بعد؟
khudh tamr wiyya l-finjān. tabi baʿad?
Have some dates with your cup. Would you like more?
B
بس، مشكور طال عمرك
bas, mashkūr ṭāl ʿumrak
That's enough, thank you, sir.
A
العفو. ما شاء الله، يعرف يهز الفنجان مثل الكبار!
il-ʿafu. mā shāʼ allāh, yaʿarf yhizz il-finjān mithil il-kbār!
You're welcome. Well done, he knows to shake the cup like the old folk!
items: a coffee cup (small, without a handle)
UAE also: finyān (فنيان); the cup: il-finjān
to a woman: ṣubbī-lah (صبي له); pour for me: ṣubb-li (صب لي)
to a woman: tfaẓẓali igʿidi (تفضلي اقعدي)
I love it, I like it (a feminine thing: coffee, a city); I love her
would you like more? (to a man)
to a woman: tabīn baʿad? (تبين بعد؟)
that's enough, thanks (said to a man)
to a woman: bas, mashkūra; in the majlis, shake the cup as you say it
he shakes the cup (to say 'no more coffee')
culture: Arabic coffee is poured a little at a time into a small finjān. Take it with your right hand. Your cup is filled again until you give it a small shake from side to side as you hand it back: that means 'no more, thank you'. One to three cups is usual.

title: Sorry, uncle!
goal: Bū Rāshid asks about your studies and you knock your cup over: say sorry and offer to clean up
tip: To say sorry, say is-samūḥa; the reply is masmūḥ 'you're forgiven'. ma ʿalēh 'never mind' means the same as maʿlēsh. Imperative + object: khallah 'leave it', khallni amsaḥah 'let me wipe it'.
grammar: recycle: imperatives with object endings (khallah, khallni amsaḥah)
dialogue: A
شو تدرس يا ولدي؟
shu tidris yā wildi?
What are you studying, son?
B
أدرس هندسة في الجامعة، طال عمرك
adris handasa fi l-jāmʿa, ṭāl ʿumrak
I'm studying engineering at the university, sir.
A
ما شاء الله عليك يا حبيبي!
mā shāʼ allāh ʿalēk yā ḥabībi!
Good for you, my dear boy!
B
الله يبارك فيك. السموحة يا عمي! طاح الفنجان
allāh ybārik fīk. is-samūḥa yā ʿammi! ṭāḥ il-finjān
Thank you. Oh, I'm so sorry, uncle! The cup's fallen over.
A
مسموح، مسموح! ما صار شي
masmūḥ, masmūḥ! ma ṣār shay
That's all right, that's all right! It's nothing.
B
خلني أمسحه يا عمي
khallni amsaḥah yā ʿammi
Let me wipe it up, uncle.
A
ما عليه، خله! سيف بيمسحه
ma ʿalēh, khallah! Sēf biyimsaḥah
Never mind, leave it! Sēf will wipe it up.
items: the reply is masmūḥ; also is-samūḥa minnak 'forgive me' (to a man; to a woman: is-samūḥa minnich)
that's all right, you're forgiven (the reply to is-samūḥa)
maʿlēsh (معليش) means the same; you'll see written ماعليه
my dear, mate (elders and friends say it to you; you say it to friends only)
usually yā ḥabībi; never to a woman outside the family
what are you studying? (to a man)
to a woman: shu tidrisīn? (شو تدرسين؟)
it fell, it fell over; he fell
let me wipe it (up) (to a man)
to a woman: khallīni amsaḥah (خليني أمسحه)
leave it, let it be (to a man)

title: Incense, and stay for dinner
goal: Bū Rāshid passes you the incense burner and insists you stay for dinner
tip: Object endings sit on imperatives: garribah ṣōbak 'bring it close to you'. tbakhkhar 'perfume yourself with incense' is an imperative too. bala means 'without': bala ʿasha 'without dinner'. bititʿashsha wiyyāna 'you'll have dinner with us' is a friendly order.
grammar: recycle: imperatives (tbakhkhar, khudh) and object endings (garribah)
dialogue: A
تفضل، هذا بخور. تبخر يا ولدي
tfaẓẓal, hādha bukhūr. tbakhkhar yā wildi
Here, this is incense. Perfume yourself with it, son.
B
ما شاء الله، ريحته حلوة وايد!
mā shāʼ allāh, rīḥtah ḥilwa wāyid!
Wow, it smells really nice!
A
خذ المدخن وقربه صوبك
khudh il-madkhan w garribah ṣōbak
Take the burner and hold it close to you.
B
زين جي يا عمي؟
zēn chī yā ʿammi?
Like this, uncle?
A
هيه، زين جي. والحين بتتعشى ويانا يا حبيبي
hē, zēn chī. w il-ḥīn bititʿashsha wiyyāna yā ḥabībi
Yes, that's right. And now you're having dinner with us, my boy.
B
الله يخليك طال عمرك، المرة الياية إن شاء الله
allāh ykhallīk ṭāl ʿumrak, il-marra l-yāya in shāʼ allāh
That's very kind, sir, next time, God willing.
A
لا والله، ما تروح بلا عشا!
la wallāh, ma trūḥ bala ʿasha!
No way, you're not leaving without dinner!
items: incense (wood chips or paste burnt for scent)
perfume yourself with the incense (to a man)
bring it closer (a masculine thing) (to a man)
to a woman: garribīh (قربيه); garribah ṣōbak 'bring it close to you'
is this all right? like this?
the answer: hē, zēn chī 'yes, that's right'
you'll have dinner with us (to a man)
to a woman: bititʿashshīn wiyyāna (بتتعشين ويانا)
you're not going (a host insisting) (to a man)
to a woman: ma trūḥīn (ما تروحين)
culture: Bukhūr (incense) is passed round in a burner, and guests let the smoke reach their clothes and hair. It often comes near the end of a visit, but it doesn't always mean the visit is over. A host will insist you stay to eat; il-marra l-yāya and allāh ykhallīk decline politely. You may also hear kaththar khērak (كثر خيرك) used as a polite 'no, thank you'.

title: Taking our leave
goal: After dinner, you and Sēf take your leave of Bū Rāshid: the long goodbye
tip: To a group, imperatives add -u: igʿid → igʿdu 'sit, stay (you all)'. -na can mean 'us', tzūrna 'you visit us', or end a past verb as 'we', sawwēna 'we did'. Leaving takes a few rounds: you say nistaʼdhin, the host says wēn? badri!, you give a reason and thank him.
dialogue: B
يا عمي، نستأذن الحين
yā ʿammi, nistaʼdhin il-ḥīn
Uncle, we'll be on our way now.
A
وين؟ بدري! اقعدوا شوي
wēn? badri! igʿdu shwayy
What, already? It's early! Stay a bit longer.
B
الله يخليك، عندي محاضرة الصبح
allāh ykhallīk, ʿindi muḥāẓra ṣ-ṣubḥ
That's kind of you, but I've got a lecture in the morning.
A
زين. حياك أي وقت، لازم تزورنا يا حبيبي
zēn. ḥayyāk ay wagt, lāzim tzūrna yā ḥabībi
All right. You're welcome any time, you must visit us, my boy.
B
أكيد إن شاء الله. ما قصرت طال عمرك
akīd in shāʼ allāh. mā gaṣṣart ṭāl ʿumrak
Of course, God willing. Thank you for everything, sir.
A
ما سوينا شي. سلم لي على أبوك، وفي أمان الله
mā sawwēna shay. sallim-li ʿala ubūk, w fī amān illāh
It was nothing. Give my regards to your father, and goodbye.
B
إن شاء الله. مع السلامة يا عمي
in shāʼ allāh. maʿa s-salāma yā ʿammi
I will. Goodbye, uncle.
items: we'll be going, we'd like to take our leave (polite)
what, already? it's early! (urging a guest to stay)
إلى أين؟ ما زال الوقت مبكرًا
to one man: igʿid (اقعد); to one woman: igʿidi (اقعدي); UAE also: iylisu (ايلسوا)
I've got a lecture, I've got a class
you visit us, (that) you visit us (to a man)
to a woman: tzūrīnna (تزورينا); lāzim tzūrna 'you must visit us'
ḥayyāk ay wagt 'you're welcome any time' (to a man)
give my regards to, say hi to … for me (to a man)
to a woman: sallmī-li ʿala (سلمي لي على)
your dad, your father (to a man)
culture: Leaving a majlis is a small ritual with several rounds. You say you're going, the host urges you to stay, you give a reason and thank him, and he asks you to come again and sends greetings to your family.
